Selma Lagerlöf (1858–1940)

Louise Vinge

Translated by Alice Burman 

Selma Lagerlöf (1858–1940)

Selma Lagerlöf and her work

Late in her life, Selma Lagerlöf wrote three autobiographical novels, all connected with the family manor Mårbacka in Värmland. That is where she grew up, surrounded by a big family and with many relations, and her primary interest in the novels is the history and the stories of the manor. Her narrated childhood is overshadowed by a hip injury that gave her a bothersome limp. In the last part, the reader finds a fourteen-year-old seeing her future task clearly, but who also feels that Mårbacka, its people and its way of life have set her outlook on life.

By emphasising the richly traditional milieu of Mårbacka and her early feeling of having a mission, Selma Lagerlöf underscored an impression that already existed in the public eye, the impression that she had inherited tales and stories and was mediating them directly through heart and memory. Modern research, however, gives another picture. It shows that the path went through rigorous education and a goal-orientated development of her abilities. Her attention to how art is constructed, the contemporary social and political problems and her awareness of the practical aspects of authorship is now obvious to any reader. It is important to emphasise that this storyteller from Värmland was an educated, well-read and well-travelled professional, with excellent language skills and critical depth. Only with this knowledge, can one truly understand her originality, her ability to capture the reader, and her immense success.

With time, Selma Lagerlöf came to be seen as one of the nation’s big personalities and a worldwide celebrity. The 1909 Nobel Prize in Literature, membership in the Swedish Academy 1914 and onwards and numerous other honours came to her. In that position, she wrote the reminiscences from Mårbacka – the home that she was then modernising to the house that today serves as a memorial estate.

Childhood, youth and studies

The three girls of Mårbacka – Anna, Selma and Gerda – got a traditional upbringing in the home. They were taught by competent governesses who encouraged Selma’s will to study. Furthermore, she got to spend time with relatives in Stockholm in order to receive treatment for her limp, and often had the opportunity to visit the theatre and opera. Her love for theatre was awoken and stayed with her throughout her life. It took the expression in theatre games, and one of the oldest of her possessions to be preserved is a puppet show that she put together as a nineteen-year-old in order to amuse herself and her sister. She made up fairy tales with elaborate plots and a language influenced by the Swedish romanticists as well as by Goethe and French storytellers.

She was also successful with occasional verse, and a speech in verse she performed at a wedding was a turning point. Among the guests were Eva Fryxell, a writer engaged in the womens’ movement. She believed that the girl ought to receive higher education. At Mårbacka the economic situation had worsened, but Eva Fryxell’s encouragement was heeded. The universities were still a world for men alone, and Selma’s eldest brother Daniel studied medicine at Uppsala. However, there was still opportunity for young women to receive vocational education at an academic level, at the Royal Women’s Teaching Academy in Stockholm. Selma Lagerlöf left Mårbacka in 1881, already twenty-three years old, in order to apply. After a year of preparation, she passed in the autumn of 1882 the training college’s entrance examination. Her father did not feel able to support her, but she persevered against his will. In spring 1885 she finished with good grades the three-year course to become a teacher. With this degree she was able to support herself, which was particularly important because Mårbacka had to be sold and the mother and aunt, who belonged to the household, had to be supported by the children.

Lagerlöf’s four years of study in Stockholm were significant. They gave a fine education in the arts, and she studied numerous subjects with teachers who introduced her to the modern ideas of the 1880s and contemporary European literature. She got many friends and was inspired for her own writing. She wrote in verse; theatrical experiences and portraits of friends were expressed in the form of sonnets or longer versified tales. According to her own accounts, it was then she realised what marvellous material she had inherited in the form of stories and memories from Värmland in the olden days. Nonetheless, she had not yet found her literary form; for a long time she wanted to write verse stories in the style of Runeberg or Snoilsky, established members of the Swedish canon, who wrote epic poems with historical and national themes.

The teacher and the first novel

In 1885 she got a position as teacher at a girls’ school in Landskrona. At first she found the small industrial town boring, but she soon found friends among her colleagues and became a part of the social life of the town. During this period, she was making an effort with her writing. The material from a historical Värmland was far from the realism demanded in the 1880s. She wanted to write about vivid characters, about passions, great gestures and wild adventures, and paint dramatic scenes with room for fantasy and madness. Fairytale and magic played a part in the story about the defrocked priest Gösta Berling and the other “cavaliers” of Ekeby, who take over the manor and drive it to its doom – and its resurrection. The abandonment of the artistic life is juxtaposed with the demands and responsibilities of work. This required a certain literary style, and she found it partly in lyrical prose, at times ironically exaggerated, mixed with lucid and fast-paced passages. The freestanding chapters gave the story a novella-like structure, made up of independent blocks that were still bound together in a complete entity. The structure had its roots in her special liking of reading aloud, where the rounded off style of the novella worked well.

While she was working on her novel, the magazine Idun announced a prize competition and she sent in five chapters of what would become Gösta Berling’s Saga (Gösta Berlings saga). She won the competition, and with the support of, among others, her older mentor in Stockholm, Sophie Adlersparre, who like Eva Fryxell belonged to the women’s movement, she was given a leave of absence and finished the novel. It was published in 1891 to mixed reviews. Many found it odd, while others, such as Gustaf Fröding, an author colleague who made his literary debut the same year, saw its audacity and originality.

Landskrona was not as isolated as it might seem. It was close to Copenhagen, where she made valuable acquaintances in intellectual circles. There were reading soirées, and she was put in contact with translators. In January 1893, Gösta Berling’s Saga was reviewed by Georg Brandes, and this opened many paths for her. She wrote numerous short stories for newspaper publication, some of which were included in the collection Invisible Links (Osynliga länkar), which was published in 1894 to favourable reviews.

In 1894, Selma Lagerlöf got to know Sophie Elkan, a wealthy lady from Gothenburg and an established author. Their friendship deepened quickly, and they were soon planning a long visit abroad with Italy as the final destination. They left autumn 1895. Lagerlöf funded her expenses by the money she had earned from the short story collection and with a travel bursary from the court. She was again given a leave of absence. Lagerlöf and Elkan travelled around for almost a year. It was truly a grand tour – they visited museums, theatres, churches and lectures. They spent a long time in the Sicilian town Taormina, and it was there Selma Lagerlöf collected material for her second novel, The Miracles of Antichrist (1897, Antikrists mirakler). In this piece, she depicts issues such as contemporary social movements, the modernisation of the countryside and child labour. This is woven together with scenes from Sicilian everyday life and a love story. The novel is about ordinary people who do things or make decisions that seem grand, responsible and mastering the self. The false image of Christ provides a double view of socialism, which appears to act for people’s material welfare but which also leaves them in a God-denying wasteland.

From The Tale of a Manor and Other Sketches to Jerusalem

In the autumn of 1897, Selma Lagerlöf left the teaching profession. She settled as an independent author in Falun, where her married sister Gerda was living. She stayed there until 1910, but even after leaving, she often returned and she wrote many of her works there. In Falun she got to know Valborg Olander, a teacher at the town’s training college. Olander became a significant part of her life and came to competently take the role of ‘writer’s wife’, as Lagerlöf jokingly put it.

Like her contemporaries, Selma Lagerlöf had a great interest in spiritual life. She read modern psychology and texts about what is healthy and what is not, what is common and what is irrational. Beginning with The Tale of a Manor (1899, En herrgårdssägen), her characterisations deepened. The novel deals with two young people who save each other from ruin. Gunnar Hede is one of these, a student who while trying to save the family finances meets with catastrophe, which results in the death of a big hoard of goats. His strange behaviour towards animals gives him the name Billy Goat. The other character is Ingrid Berg who met him as a thirteen-year-old and was unable to forget him. She is lovelessly treated in a foster-home, falls into depression and is believed to be dead. In one melodramatic scene, she is saved from the grave she was put in by Hede. By a coincidence she comes to Hede’s home, a decayed manor where sorrow is in control and the mother hopes that Ingrid would save the son. It is a long struggle, but finally Ingrid manages to convince him to want to become well and live with her. With its strong scenes, as well as its studies of the spiritual life and love’s sometime spiritual communications, the story gained great success.

The Queens of Kungahälla and Other Sketches (Drottningar i Kungahälla), historical tales from the Middle Ages, was also published in 1899. In Herr Arne’s Hoard (Herr Arnes penningar) she made use of material from Bohuslän, inspired by numerous summer visits in Kungälv where her brother Daniel was the town doctor. It is a short novel, dealing with a young woman who is tempted to love or believe to love a man who has killed her relatives, among them a beloved foster sister. She shies away from the demands of justice, but ultimately has to betray him and give her life to make up for her mistake. The story was based on a real incident in the 1570s, but Lagerlöf has added the love story, the vengeful dead who haunt the couple as well as a magical connection between the guilty consciences and the changeable winter weather. This gives the piece both cosmic dimensions and psychological depth. The story is written in the laconic and rough style of the Icelandic sagas, which resonates well with the content.

Herr Arne’s Hoard was serialised in 1903 and published in a single volume in 1904. Lagerlöf wrote it as relaxation while working on a bigger project. She had been reading about peasants in Dalecarlia who for religious reasons had emigrated from Nås to Palestine in 1896. During her long travels with Sophie Elkan in 1899-1900, she visited their colony in Jerusalem, between their journeys to Egypt and Turkey. When she returned from her travels she wrote about the peasants in the two-volume novel Jerusalem (1901-1902, re-worked edition published in 1909). The first part has the subtitle “In Dalecarlia” and is about the rise of revivalism in a district where the respected Ingmarssönerna were for years in a prominent position. Willpower, responsibility and a sense of justice are the traits that characterise them, and from the start one sees people who face difficult decisions and do big, selfless actions. In the centre is a love story that is complicated by money, which leads to betrayal. Fanaticism and ruin is depicted as well as group pressure and solidarity in the district torn apart by the revivalism. Loyalty towards the native district is put against faith and the hope to meet Christ in the Holy Land.

In the second part, “In the Holy Land”, guilt and the spirit of self-sacrifice moves the plot forward. Estrangement, the strain from the weather and the meetings with the relationships in the colony is depicted. The hardships of the new life are balanced with the joy of being in Jerusalem, the comfort of the colony and the happiness for personal development. Admiration for the brave emigrants and their faith characterises the story, but here is also a great distance from their extreme behaviour.

The Wonderful Adventures of Nils

Jerusalem was, with its themes of home and emigration and its powerful peasant types, right for the time. Selma Lagerlöf had begun to be internationally successful, particularly in Germany, and now her authorship spread over the whole of Europe. The German audience appreciated the rustic and provincial as a countermovement against the country’s industrialisation and city misery.

Her next story was spread even further, even though it was a novel written in a national spirit: The Wonderful Adventures of Nils (1906-1907, Nils Holgerssons underbara resa genom Sverige). The book was commissioned for use in the elementary school in 1901, and while they had expected a conventional novel, they got something quite different. When the author at last, after a long time of inactivity, dragged-out research trips and comprehensive material collection, started writing, the story was shaped from a combination of her own and others’ concepts, themes and ideas. The novel was an adventure novel, a piece of travel writing as well as a bildungsroman, and it was influenced by fairytales and fables. The idea of having a young person who was able to talk to animals and gain his life stance from them came from Rudyard Kipling.

Nils Holgersson is at the start of the novel a mean and unreliable teenager. He is punished by being enchanted into an elf, one hand’s breadth tall. In this miniature format he is dragged along on the wild geese’s northbound trip by a young gander Mårten. Nils is at once put through a number of tests that show that camaraderie and solidarity are necessary for his survival and ability to help Mårten. The two are accepted by the flock of geese that is run by the stern old Akka from Kebnekajse. The adventure starts and Nils gets to see all of Sweden, and learns about its appearance, history and people. The enchantment is shameful, but there is pleasure in the life lived together with the animals. The boy also has to encounter the difficult sides of life; depression and sorrow is remarkable often depicted when encountering people and animals. In the autumn Nils manages to get back to his home together with Mårten gander, but once he is there, he is faced with a terrible decision. If he brings Mårten home, he can become a person again, but Mårten has to be slaughtered. The goose gets caught, and at last Nils defies his shame and stops his mother, who is ready with a knife in her hand. The enchantment is broken and he stands as a full-grown man in his mother’s arms. Again we see the grand gesture of self-mastery, but now in a youthful demeanour.

There were quite some argumentative discussions about The Wonderful Adventures of Nils. Should children really read such fantastical stories? Nevertheless, the novel was used for many years in schools, sometimes jerkily read aloud, but most of the time appreciated. Translations and re-workings were spread across the globe. In these the teenager is commonly reduced to a little child. With this, the serious nature of his task and his development disappears, as does the novel’s celebration of the developing modern Swedish language. As a result, Selma Lagerlöf is in many countries only seen as a children’s writer.

This impression was enforced by the short story collection Christ Legends and Other Stories (Kristuslegender) from 1904, which also was widely spread in translation. Its legends, taken from among others Jesus’ life, seem simple, but demand much from the reader’s ability to enter into the text. Here are some of Selma Lagerlöf’s best known short stories, such as ”In Nazareth” (“I Nazaret”) and ”Robin Redbreast” (“Fågel Rödbröst”).

Back to Mårbacka. The Nobel Prize in Literature

Lagerlöf’s success brought with it sizeable earnings and in 1907, she bought back Mårbacka. At first, she only took over a then dilapidated house, but soon she also got the grounds. The overhaul began the following year, but she waited with the big refurbishment until the 1920s.

In 1908, Selma Lagerlöf turned fifty. Her position in the cultural sphere was evidenced through celebration articles, great gifts and festivities. Carl Larsson painted her portrait. She published a book, The Girl from March Croft and Other Stories (En saga om en saga och andra sagor), where she writes about her debut as an author and thanks those who supported her from the start. The collection also contains a number of shorter stories as well as the longer “The Girl from the Marsh Croft” (“Tösen från Stormyrtorpet”). This story is about a young woman who has given birth to an illegitimate child; the father is the son in the house where she works as a maid. The matter is taken to the district court, and when he is just about to swear that the child is not his, she yanks away the Bible in order to prevent him from committing perjury. After many twists and turns, she is finally made his wife. The melodramatic and folkloristic romanticism in the story appealed to the audiences and it is not surprising that it was the first of the author’s stories to be made into a film, which was released in 1917.

At this point, Selma Lagerlöf had been a contender for the Nobel Prize in Literature for a few years. The disagreements surrounding The Wonderful Adventures of Nils made her controversial, but the resistance was crushed and in 1909 she was awarded the prize. Her acceptance speech at the banquet was full of joy. The speech was an imagined conversation with her father about the many people she had to thank for her successes and all the debts that she had to unburden herself from. The speech was plain and moving, and surprisingly humorous.

Liljecrona’s Home and Thy Soul Shall Bear Witness!

Mårbacka played a part in the acceptance speech, and the estate is also featured in Liljecrona’s Home (1911, Liljecronas hem), where it is serves as the framework of the story of her paternal grandparents’ lives. It is a love story with fairytale elements – the wicked stepmother, a water nymph, has exerted her power over the kind father – and the young heroine has to use both cunning and power to reach her goal. Some moments of the story are carried by a forceful realism, others by a burlesque humour; pictures from the old Värmland, both the flourishing woman’s life in the home and its male world of hunting and adventure, makes the novel particularly interesting.

With the Nobel Prize of Literature, Selma Lagerlöf became a prominent figure in numerous contexts, not least in the fight for women’s suffrage. As the main speaker at the sixth international Women’s Suffrage congress in 1911, she delivered the speech “Home and state”. The speech was carefully worked through, presenting arguments both for and against women playing a part in politics and professional work outside the home. The final closing remark was as follows: ‘The little masterpiece, the home, was our creation with the help from man. The great masterpiece, the state, will be made by man, when he seriously takes on woman as his helper.’ She held a number of other speeches for the movement, before suffrage was finally won in 1919.

Lagerlöf’s position in Scandinavia was manifested in 1912, when she was invited to deliver a speech on the Society of Swedish Literature in Finland’s Runeberg Day celebrations, taking place on the fifth of February. From Helsinki, Lagerlöf travelled onwards to Saint Petersburg and Moscow. There were countless celebrations, parties and meetings with interesting people. In 1912 she also published the short novel Thy Soul Shall Bear Witness! (Körkarlen). The novel was commissioned by The National Society Against Tuberculosis, and consists of a combination of original ideas and well-known motifs. The plot is based on a French story about a ghost who collects the souls of the dying, but it is combined with a trope most notably used in Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol, where a stingy man is forced to see the consequences of his virulent actions during a magical Christmas night.

The protagonist of Thy Soul Shall Bear Witness!, David Holm, is a brute and a wife beater, a formerly impressive man who has fallen victim to alcoholism. He has ended up in a small town where the Salvation Army is attempting to save fallen women. Sister Edith is attracted to him and does what she can to help, but meets only scorn. She catches his tuberculosis and is on the brink of death when David, himself dying, is made to travel through the New Year’s Eve night in a phantom carriage and has to see his victims. When he reaches sister Edith, he realises her love and humiliates himself with a feeling of bliss, because he finds himself to be so loved. In a dramatic finale he returns as a penitent to his wife to put away his hatred, with Edith’s spirit to help him. It is in the eleventh hour, when his wife stands ready to kill her children and take her life. The couple reconcile and the story finishes on a note of sad resignation as well as hope.

In Thy Soul Shall Bear Witness!, Lagerlöf engrossed herself in the borderline world between life and death which she became more and more fascinated by. Spiritism and theosophy interested her, but she was searching out for herself a sustainable way of life and a satisfactory explanation for the divine. Thy Soul Shall Bear Witness! was made into a film that was successful thanks to the fact that it was already technically possible to visualise the in-between state that implies the interaction between life and death, as well as the fact that Viktor Sjöström was able to do justice to the story’s hatred, love and atonement.

The Emperor of Portugallia and The Outcast

In the early summer of 1914, Selma Lagerlöf became the first woman elected to be a member of the Swedish Academy. Her predecessor on chair seven was Albert Theodor Gellerstedt, a sympathetic but hardly exciting person, whom she was required to honour in a speech. The same year, she wrote The Emperor of Portugallia (Kejsarn av Portugallien), one of the highlights of her writing career. The tale is set in the Värmland of the 1860s and is characterised by an episodic narration. A number of stories show how the inconspicuous crofter Jan in Skrolycka gets a daughter and how he takes to fatherhood with a pride that turns into hubris and complete madness.

One of the characteristics of Selma Lagerlöf’s farmers’ world is the importance of reputation. Jan is not well-reputed in the least, and he knows it. Being the father of a beautiful girl gives him some standing. But Klara Gulla, his daughter, wants to see the world, partly to earn money for the parents, who are in financial difficulties. She manages to help them, but when Jan gets told that it was not done honourably, he denies her moral fall and instead raises her to the skies. He becomes the Emperor, the father of the ‘Empress of Portugallia’, a madman who despite it all wins respect for his personal dignity.

Klara Gulla returns after many years. She has survived well, but she has been coarsened both in behaviour and looks. She wants to bring her parents to her new home, but distances herself from her father when she realises that he is mad. Instead, she tries to bring only her mother with her. Jan scrambles after them to the boat jetty and throws himself into the lake. For a long while, Klara Gulla searches for her drowned father with a guilt that turns into terror. In the end, her mother dies and Jan is found again. The final scene shows Klara Gulla’s atonement, deepening self-understanding and her return to the parish community.

Jan in Skrolycka returns in two later short story collections, The Changeling I and II (1915 and 1921, Troll och människor I och II). In these collections, some of Selma Lagerlöf’s best-known short stories can be found. Many of the stories deal with the secret and threatening relationship between man and nature, such as ”Vattnet i Kyrkviken”, “Bortbytingen” and “Tomten på Töreby”. In these collections she also published several of her speeches and reflections, such as one about the powerlessness felt with regards to World War One, ”Rakels gråt”.

The tragedies of the First World War affected Selma Lagerlöf greatly and got its literary expression in the novel The Outcast (1918, Bannlyst). Critics have struggled with this novel, where the different plots are pressed together, but the main idea of the story is simple: war is shameful and disgusting. This disgust makes Sven Elversson, one of the novel’s main characters, into a problematic hero, because his miserable reputation always precedes him despite his will to do good. The vicar’s wife Sigrun is married to a controlling husband, whom she runs away from. However, she is only partly believable in her goodness, and the priest Rhånge, with his inheritance of blame, shame and violence seems more than anything a symbolic representation of the evil in man’s world. As with David Holm, Rhånge is converted in the end. The novel is set in Bohuslän, and the people’s temperament and religiosity is used as a background for the atmosphere that the events rest upon. The surrounding mountains are used in order to portray Sigrun’s feelings of isolation and confinement.

Autobiographical

The Swedish Academy had at one point commissioned Lagerlöf to write a biography on the Finlander Zacharias Topelius. The subject was not close to her heart, and the intimate name form in the title, Zachris Topelius (1920), seems to imply that it was his childhood that interested her the most. It is possible that this biography is the reason why she returned to the world of her own childhood in Mårbacka: The Story of a Manor (Mårbacka) in 1922, Memories of my Childhood: Further Years at Mårbacka (Ett barns memoarer) in 1930 and The Diary of Selma Lagerlöf (Dagbok för Selma Ottilia Lovisa Lagerlöf) in 1932. Lagerlöf had already written autobiographically in ”En saga om en saga” and ”Två spådomar”; she had spoken of Mårbacka at the Nobel dinner; she had presented it as Lövdala in Gösta Berling’s Saga, Liljecrona’s Home and The Emperor of Portugallia, and the manor features in the chapter “A Little Homestead” in The Wonderful Adventures of Nils.

The theme of losing one’s home is central in writings such as The Tale of a Manor, Herr Arne’s Hoard and Jerusalem. It is clear that this is one of Lagerlöf’s main themes. Mårbacka meant family and traditions, and signified a calm and good life close to animals and nature, but also a cultural tradition of music, reading and being together both in the everyday and at special occasions. The autobiographical pieces are not always happy, as the child and the young girl is struck again and again by feelings of threat and doom, notions of the complications of being grown up, and the budding realisations of the power and pain of love.

The Ring trilogy

Between the publications of Mårbacka and Memories of my Childhood, Lagerlöf wrote a series of novels, The Löwensköld Ring (Löwensköldska ringen), Charlotte Löwensköld and Anna Svärd. The first two were published in 1925, with the final novel being published in 1928, the year Selma Lagerlöf turned seventy. The Ring trilogy takes its scene in the eighteenth century and has a seat farm in Värmland as the main place of action. It is a ghost story with similarities to Herr Arne’s Hoard. General Löwensköld fought in Charles XII’s army, and as a reward for his services, the king gives him a ring, which, like the treasure of Herr Arne, is connected with violence and unfruitful times. After it is stolen from the general’s grave, there are numerous accidents that are blamed on the dead man. The hidden journeys of the ring, the ghoul’s vengefulness and people’s romantic tragedies are woven together to an exciting diegesis. A young woman manages to return the ring to the ghost – but the expected reward is never given. As with many other works by Lagerlöf, this novel shows self-mastery that leads to atonement, but the eerie effects of the ghost story is in the foreground.

The next two novels are realistically designed, but the family curse features and still rules the family’s fate. One of the main characters is Karl-Artur Ekenstedt, who is studying to become a priest and through self-obsession and spiritual blindness is heading in the horrifying direction of decay. Set against Karl-Artur, one finds his cousin and fiancée, Charlotte Löwensköld, who is an impulsive and charming young woman with integrity and a sense of justice. She loves Karl-Artur but is parted from him through thoughtlessness and his easily wounded sense of pride. Her story is full of humour and light. Lagerlöf’s psychological interest is found mostly in the multifaceted depiction of the enchanting but dominant colonel’s wife Ekenstedt, Karl-Artur's mother, and Charlotte’s involvement in the strained relationship between mother and son. She overcomes indignities and trials, and finally gets a fine man in a marriage of convenience that turns into deep love.

Anna Svärd has as its heroine a woman from another class, a Dalecarlian peasant girl, whom Karl-Artur marries in desperation without any respect for the way she views marriage. She is upright, clear-sighted and practical, but his inability to understand her needs in the unequal marriage is devastating. Furthermore, he has come under the influence of another woman who ultimately pulls him into a travelling gypsy lifestyle. Her name is Thea Sundler and she is the daughter of the woman who appeased the ghost in The Löwensköld Ring. Here the Löwensköld family fate comes to light in a violent catastrophe. Sections of brilliant humour are juxtaposed against a dark backdrop where meanness and maliciousness are given room to play.

Selma Lagerlöf’s sharp observations of lifestyles, norms and values in various social classes gives this trilogy a special interest and depth. Reputation plays a key part; it hangs together with stability, honesty and being willing to work, and it must be carefully cared for. The trilogy also shows how titles and positions affect manor lives. The psychological insight reaches its peak in the representation of the Ekenstedt family and in the characterisation of Thea Sundler. When Lagerlöf depicts Thea’s manipulations and the blinding love the colonel’s wife feels for her son, she shows an attitude towards women with certain less attractive aspects. Power play in familial and romantic relationships is presented without any sentimentality. Karl-Artur is the least appealing of Selma Lagerlöf’s many priests. She made a brave decision when she put such an unsympathetic man in the centre of her story and did not allow him a spiritual breakthrough toward realisation and love. Whether he manages to redeem himself is unclear: Selma Lagerlöf tried to continue the series, but it remained unfinished.

The final phase of a long authorship

Harvest (Höst), a collection of short stories, memories and speeches, was published in 1933. In this one can find important illustrations of her early years and success, moving episodes about Mårbacka and her closest relatives and glimpses of her life in Värmland. Also featured is the story ”Skriften på jordgolvet”, which was originally published to support the refugees from Nazi Germany. This led to a political campaign against her from the Germans, but Lagerlöf supported the Jews.

For her seventy-fifth birthday in 1933, Bonniers decided to publish Selma Lagerlöf’s works in a collected suite. Lagerlöf insisted that the language should be modernised and made more colloquial, particularly in the dialogue. This was in line with her interest in depicting language – in her later works one finds a style that is based on a narrating, precise colloquial speech. Stylistic features that she experimented with during her early years as a writer, such as the lyrical aspects in Gösta Berling’s Saga or the impressionistic painting in some of her novellas was abandoned for a simpler style. The Icelandic saga’s laconic form might be a model, but there were other routes to a natural narration. She frequently used the Värmland dialect in her drafts to find the right intonation, and sometimes she let her characters speak in dialect. One can also see that she often lets her characters tell and listen to stories. Later on, humour and irony became more and more noticeable elements in her books.

The characteristic elements in Selma Lagerlöf’s storytelling – both her style and content – differ from her contemporaries. She portrays people in many dimensions – spiritual, psychological, moral – and she enjoyed in putting them against supernatural powers, who support or demand submission from them. Stern righteousness and revenge is apparent, as well as sacrificial love and wise insight. The existential side is always anchored in realistic settings, some of which are more important than others. The church is one important setting, in which Lagerlöf often considers how the norm of ‘reputation’ works. Another place for big collective scenes is the market, where colourful and violent episodes take place and where male initiative and drama stands in the foreground. In the home, the woman can be found in the kitchen, where she works on her intimately described tasks, but there are also chambers where she can sit on her own or alone with someone else. In manors, events take place in the drawing room and dining room where the characters will narrate or read for one another. The rooms are described in detail, but Lagerlöf does not paint historical interiors for their own sake, but to connect them with characters and situations. Her characters are rarely passive. They travel far and bravely, and many sections are set on roads, in carriages or on walks, situations where the senses are tested, characters become evident and where transitions and changes can occur.

Today, it is almost impossible to imagine Selma Lagerlöf’s world reputation. Her books were translated to countless languages, her stories were dramatised and filmed, and her life was described in albums and in biographies even while she was alive. Her fan mail was enormous; the tourists visiting Mårbacka plenty. She became, to a certain extent, a prisoner of her fame, but was able to escape to Falun and the home that she kept for her sister’s family. Selma Lagerlöf died on the sixteenth of March in 1940 on Mårbacka. The funeral was a matter of state, and the restoration of Mårbacka to a memorial estate of her and her works, which happened according to her testament, became the inevitable continuation of her will as an author.
